title: Overwatch's old battle passes are finally coming back permanently starting next month, but some of the rewards will be left out
summary: After years, Blizzard is loosening up on the battle pass FOMO.
body: Overwatch's next season will finally move the hero shooter more in line with the other live service games that don't purely rely on FOMO for their battle passes. In season 4, Blizzard will "unvault" an old battle pass and make it available again. The details on how exactly the system will work are slim at the moment, but it sounds like a specific old battle pass will become available halfway through every season going forward. It will be on sale for anyone who doesn't own it or simply made available for anyone who paid for it previously, and it will be permanent from that point on. There is one catch however: The premium currency, player titles, and Mythic-level skins that were in old battle passes won't be available in the new unvaulted versions. Overwatch used to have new heroes locked behind a tier in the old battle passes too, but I am guessing they've been replaced with a generic reward. Blizzard says there will be more information about exactly how these will work closer to the halfway point of the season, which will be sometime next month. Ditching some of the FOMO involved with battle passes is always a welcome change in my book. It's a little sad that it won't be every ba…

title: Payday has come to Fortnite, because today's cool gamers are 'discovering legendary IPs in entirely new ways'
summary: The new game is called, literally and in totality, Heist Escape Roguelike: Payday Experience.
body: The ongoing effort to come up with a new Payday game that people actually want to play continued today with the announcement of Heist Escape Roguelike: Payday Experience, a UEFN game that's available exclusively in (you guessed it) Fortnite. Heist Escape Roguelike: Payday Experience "reimagines elements of Payday as a progressive roguelike shooter," with three separate heists—the Jewelry Store, the Bank, and the Harbor—each of them made up of multiple unique rooms "ensuring endless replayability." "We recognize that today's audiences are discovering legendary IPs in entirely new ways," Starbreeze chief growth officer Matt Dixon said. "Integrating Payday into the Fortnite ecosystem through UEFN is a cornerstone of our strategy to engage new players and welcome them into the broader Payday platform." That's the sort of utterance that you're only going to hear from an entertainment industry executive, but it does nonetheless get to the heart of Starbreeze's big problem. Payday 2 , which launched in 2013, is still chugging along on Steam, with concurrent player counts that keep it consistently within the platform's 100 most-played games . But Payday 3 continues to flounder, and while …

title: Persona big boss says 'I think we have to do' remakes of the series' most-neglected games
summary: Put away your PSPs, friends.
body: We're up to our necks in Persona. Whichever entry you're keen on, there's something for you. Persona 3? Enjoy the port of Persona 3 Portable, or the Persona 3 remake, or its Episode Aigis DLC. Enjoy Persona 4? Why, that's getting a flashy remake of its own. Or maybe you're a Persona 5 fan? Revel in the veritable mountain of P5-themed stuff that is sprinkled all across videogames like the fallout of a meteor strike. Oh, unless you like Persona 1 and/or 2, of course, in which case please return to your hole and cease speaking. So it goes. Despite being the games most obviously in need of a gloss-up, Persona's PS1-era games have never gotten much love from Atlus and Sega. But maybe that could change? In a recent chat with GamerBraves , Persona series producer Kazuhisa Wada said that—so far as he's concerned—Persona 1 and 2 remakes are damn-near a necessity. "At this point, I can’t say for sure [if Persona 1 and 2 remakes will happen]," said Wada, but added that "personally, I think it’s something we should definitely do. I think we have to do it." Of course, right now, Wada and Atlus are preoccupied with Persona 4 Revival, which comes out in February next year. “Persona 4 is, persona…

title: The Steam Machine design makes for a frightfully good tissue box, and now you can 3D print your own
summary: Maybe useful to catch our tears over memory prices right now.
body: Achoo! Sorry, my hayfever's been playing up again. Let me just grab a tissue from my Steam Machine... is something you could be saying if you're willing to 3D print the replica this generous individual over on Reddit designed and shared. The Steam Machine Style Tissue Box Cover (or 'Enclosure') is, practically speaking, just a tissue box. But I'll be damned if I'm not tempted to buy a 3D printer just to make one. It looks very much like a real Steam Machine, sans all the actual gubbins that makes it, well, the real thing . You can download the 3D files from MakerWorld and have one of your own. The creator Boyso expands: "Default print profiles are meant to be used with a 0.4 mm nozzle and a smooth build plate. Additional print profiles are provided where it prints on its side for textured build plates." Boyso also explains: "To keep things authentic, I've included two print profiles: 512 GB [or] 2 TB. Just like the real thing... except they're exactly the same. Pick whichever capacity makes you feel faster." Personally, I'd be going for the 2 TB one—you just never know. Placebo effects are real, after all. I turned a Steam Machine into a tissue box. from r/steammachine One thing t…

title: 1666: Amsterdam has the makings of something brilliant but I came away from its preview with a bad feeling as its early access release creeps too close for comfort
summary: I want to play 1666: Amsterdam's final iteration, I just hope it gets that far.
body: I can think of little else cooler than flying above the streets of 17th Century Amsterdam, in the dead of night, on a broom stick, with a black cat. Looking down on the amber glow of the oil-lit streetlamps is my lasting positive memory of 1666: Amsterdam's preview, but I can't say I had the same fondness for it once I got up close and personal with what was on the ground. 1666: Amsterdam is over a decade old now, the brainchild of Patrice Désilets, director and creative lead of Assassin's Creed and co-founder of Panache. He had to fight for the game, suing his former employer Ubisoft for the rights to it. Now, he's working on it at Montreal indie-based studio Panache Digital Games. (Image credit: Panache Digital Games) "We do between 15 to 20 builds a day," Désilets explains. "So it always has to be playable, it's an iterative process at Panache. Progression is more important than perfection." A lot of progression has clearly been made in 1666: Amsterdam, what with its impressive map, interesting story, and smart exploration ideas. Even just during the preview its world felt impossibly big, but the real question is whether all these grand ideas will be polished enough for an earl…

title: The 'world's first' water-cooled Steam Machine is a Frankenstein's monster of neon pink tubing and external hardware
summary: More Franken-machines, please.
body: Although I criticised the Steam Machine for its hefty price tag upon release, part of me hoped the creator community might do something interesting with it. Lo and behold, we now have the first example of a water-cooled version —and I can't help but be impressed. The Not-so-steamy Machine (as I shall call it) is the work of Stefan Warecka , who claim's it's the "world's first" example. They've posted a short video on Reddit summarising some of the build process, which begins with... attacking the Steam Machine's carboard box with an angle grinder. Good lord. Watercooled Steam Machine Build Video from r/PcBuild Despite the "hack first and ask questions later" approach, the end product is a rather beautiful Steam Machine with a fan-cooled radiator strapped to the back, a custom CNC-ed water block, and lots of external tubing—which is then duly filled with a neon-pink liquid solution. It looks like a mini PC that's spent a long night on the Pepto-Bismol. We've all been there, folks. Warecka says that APU temps have dropped by 20-30 degrees , and a full video is coming soon to their YouTube channel . In the meantime, we can only guess at the potential performance benefits. Cyberpunk 2…

summary: Things are looking up.
body: Given the current state of the industry elsewhere— it's, uh, dire —I'm pleased to report that Square Enix, creator of the Final Fantasy series among other games, is doing pretty alright, all things considered. The news comes as a result of a financial results report, shared here by Gamebiz.jp (and translated by Automaton ). In the fiscal year ending 2027, ol' Square saw a major 88.6% operating profit increase year-on-year, mostly thanks to its videogame business—which itself saw its operating profit increase by 91.8% and its revenue by 51.8%. That's mainly due to Final Fantasy 7: Rebirth, which is finally meeting some expectations , one would surmise. What's interesting to me is the footnote that Final Fantasy 14 —a game whose popularity had been struggling with the somewhat-stagnant formula of Dawntrail, with an unofficial (but consistent and long-standing) census reporting a significant downturn back in June 2025— experienced an uptick in players in that same census earlier this year . title: Sean Murray still loves playing the 2016 version of No Man's Sky: 'It's a little bit weirder, but it's got its charm'
summary: "I've got a real soft spot for it," says the founder of Hello Games.
body: No Man's Sky has changed an awful lot in the 10 years since its launch. Hello Games' space sandbox has received a few dozen major free updates that have added features like base-building, spaceship construction, multiplayer missions, companions, mechs, and even its own version of the Death Star . Speaking to PC Gamer for No Man's Sky's 10th anniversary, Sean Murray said that despite all those massive changes and added features that have transformed the space sandbox… he still likes the 2016 version of No Man's Sky just fine. "I've gone back to the original, played the game without any updates," Murray said. "And I've got a real soft spot for it, to be honest. It's a more esoteric experience. It's a little bit weirder, but it's got its charm." "The feeling that I have when I play it is, I'm alone and I'm on a planet and I don't know what's over the hill," Murray said. "And I really love that feeling." Which isn't to say the updated No Man's Sky, even with its busy community events and multiplayer hubs, can't feel that way too. "I still get that feeling when I play No Man's Sky now," he said. "That is still in there, and is still the heart of the game. But personally, I love that I …

title: Marvel Rivals hits the Ozempic, comes back 40 GB lighter
summary: Svelte and superheroic.
body: Incredible news, folks: Marvel Rivals has completely repackaged its assets. No, not those assets . Last Friday, the internet's most erogenous shooter announced that it was slimming down. As part of an "Optimized texture resource compression strategy across all platforms," Marvel Rivals now comes in about 40 GB lighter on PC than it did before. This is part of the game's bevy of season 9.5 tweaks and updates. In a chat with a stationary camera, Marvel Rivals creative director Guangyun Chen said that "our tech wizards have been hard at work forging solutions. In season 9.5, we are implementing a massive texture compression overhaul, without sacrificing a single pixel of visual fidelity." The downside is that, because NetEase is rejigging everything, the actual season 9.5 update itself is meatier than usual. "The initial season 9.5 update will be larger than usual, but the final install size will be much lighter," says Chen. It's always nice when this happens. Last year, Helldivers 2 pulled a similar trick , chopping itself down from "~154GB to ~23GB". How? Magic. Plus, the devs at Arrowhead went and de-duped a load of data across the game's installed files. Previously, all sorts of …

title: Australians must now prove their age to buy R18+ games on the Xbox store
summary: Microsoft is the first among major games platforms to implement stricter age verification.
body: If you use the Xbox store to buy either Xbox or PC games—and yes, the latter is possible—you may be prompted to verify your age the next time you try to buy an R18+ game. Microsoft confirmed as much via emails sent to users over the weekend, which I received. "Starting August 2026, to comply with Australia regulations, you may need to verify your age before purchasing or accessing apps and games rated 18+ on Microsoft Store and Xbox Store," the email reads. To verify your age with Microsoft you can use email-based verification, a facial age estimation check via "secure selfie", a credit card or a government issued ID which can include a driver's license or passport. Verification is done via London-based tech company VerifyMy . Age verification software has come under deserved scrutiny this year. In February, security researchers claim to have found that verification provider Persona is not only lax with information security but also does a lot more than simply verify your age . Persona is among the most widely used verification providers, with Roblox, Twitch and VRChat using the software. Discord trialed it on its UK users. title: Steam Week in Review: Games about sorting 1000s of mundane objects onto shelves are the new craze sweeping PC gaming
summary: All the interesting Steam facts for the week ending August 9.
body: Games about cleaning are all the rage. The recent success of House Flipper, Power Wash Simulator and Unpacking demonstrates there's a mainstream-sized appetite among PC gamers for making messy places neat and tidy. But the micro-genre goes back way further than that. The 1982 arcade game Bubbles was about using a bubble to clean a filthy sink. Cosy foundational text Harvest Moon—like its descendant Stardew Valley—has you gradually transforming a forgotten ruin into a quaint and personalised space. Then there's stuff like Chibi-Robo and Katamari Damacy. Not all cleaning games are cosy or sim-oriented. Viscera Cleanup Detail is about cleaning blood 'n' guts and The Gunk is a 3D platformer about eliminating space gunk in order to, I'm not sure, probably save the world. And the recent wave of retail simulators have lots of cleaning and sorting. But the cleaning or tidying game has evolved once again. Its newest manifestation may clock as either a living nightmare or the height of blissful stimulation, depending on your temperament. To demonstrate, here's the trailer for Toy Shop Tidy Up , which launched on August 7: With all due respect to both the creators Shiftmoon and those enthusi…

title: Free-to-play Division game launches on Steam to mixed reviews: 'Calling it slop disrespects actual slop'
summary: The Division Resurgence was made for mobile and it shows.
body: Tom Clancy's The Division Resurgence originally launched on mobile before coming to PC via Ubisoft Connect (the artist formerly known as Uplay) in April. Earlier this month it arrived on Steam , where it hasn't received the warmest welcome. Overall its review rating is currently sitting at "mixed" with just 46% of reviews leaning to the positive. Players are frustrated by login issues, mouse bugs, and the looter-shooter's combination of underwhelming rewards and overwhelming microtransactions. "Calling it slop disrespects actual slop", says one user review. "I've seen Korean gacha games with less microtransaction than this. This is scummy even for a F2P. It has [t]he most distracting, convoluted, overcomplicated on purpose and bad thought UI and Menus design I've ever seen in a video-game. You spend more time micro-managing than playing missions!" "Complete ass game", begins another review. "Balancing is the main issue, as well as loot progression. All the loot is locked behind daily completions, and you only get to do those maybe 4-5 times a day. Then the game scales the xp and rewards down hard! This isn't a looter-shooter, its a daily log-in simulator with Division like systems…

title: The designer of Diamond City, Little Lamplight, and Starfield's Neon thinks Bethesda's galaxy was just too big: 'I would have done a handful of planets with bespoke layouts'
summary: Nate Purkeypile worked on Starfield for a year before leaving Bethesda.
body: In a new episode of The Examined Game podcast (spotted by GamesRadar ), longtime Bethesda environment artist and The Axis Unseen dev Nate Purkeypile spoke about his time at the legendary studio, including what he found to be Starfield's biggest design misstep. Purkeypile had the title of "environment artist" at Bethesda, but his work seems to have extended into what would traditionally be considered level design. In addition to setting up the layout for Starfield's city of Neon⁠—which remained largely the same in the released game, according to Purkeypile⁠—the dev spoke about his contributions to Little Lamplight and Diamond City in Fallouts 3 and 4. He left Bethesda a year into Starfield's development, and released his first solo game, The Axis Unseen , in 2024. Purkeypile spoke about the importance of deliberate design and points of interest in making areas late in the interview. "I think it's good to spend as little time as possible in menus, especially when it comes to exploration like that," said Purkeypile. Host Steven Lake asked if this was an issue Purkeypile saw coming in Starfield's development, a more disjointed, menu-driven system of travel. "It's very accurate that if…

title: Lies of P studio reveals name change and hypes up sequel: 'My goal has been to create the world's greatest action game.'
summary: Round 8 is now Nough, I think.
body: Lies of P studio Nough, formerly Round8, has released a 16-minute mini documentary about its culture and work on the Lies of P series, including development anecdotes and talk of the developers' ambitions for Lies of P's in-production sequel. But first, the name change: According to the video description, Nough is "upholding the development philosophy of Round8 Studio and operating under the motto 'Games by Gamers.'" It's not entirely clear to me whether Nough is a full rebrand of Round8, or rather spun off from the original company, itself a subsidiary of publisher Neowiz. The end result is the same as far as we're concerned, I think: The people who made Lies of P are Nough now, a portmanteau of "Not Enough." Neat. The studio is still tight lipped about the Lies of P sequel, which we know is in full production, but has yet to get a formal reveal or even name. The Nough devs were very open about their ambitions to make a bigger, better game, though. "From the very start, my goal has been to create the world's greatest action game," said combat director Lee Jeonghyeon. "And we're getting there, one step at a time." title: Deltarune's 'The Third Sanctuary' is an affront to time signatures, and also one of my favourite songs in a videogame ever
summary: The drummer will say "please" and then "make it stop".
body: Critical Hit (Image credit: Future) Welcome to Critical Hit , where Mollie (or someone else on the PC Gamer team) celebrate and lament all things videogame music, audio design, and the ways our favourite games make our ears tingle. This week I'm that "someone else", and I'm here to talk your ear off about time signatures! So I've recently given in and decided I won't be waiting for Deltarune's final chapter before I played it all in one go—too many of my mates were talking about it, so I sat my butt down to get ahead of the invariable, accidental spoilers and chew through chapters one to five. You don't need me to tell you that Toby Fox, developer of Deltarune (and Undertale preceding it) is an excellent composer. The dude made Megalovania, which has somehow survived being piledrivered into memedom, even by the Pope of all people , and still, inevitably, slaps. But the rest of his discography is flooded with bangers. The man can work a leitmotif, lemme tell ya. Deltarune is no different, though for this Soundtrack Sunday, I want to focus heavily on one song from it: The Third Sanctuary, because this song might be one of my favourite tunes in a videogame ever. summary: Hold on to that coin, actually.
body: Excited for The Witcher to finally wrap up? No, I'm not talking about that Witcher 3 playthrough you abandoned after 70 hours of wandering around, I'm talking about the Netflix show probably best known for its prominent recast of Geralt and for being very different from the books and games. Well, it's been delayed (via What's on Netflix ). Even though it reportedly wrapped filming late last year, the story from What's on Netflix says that "a little digging" confirms "that the release has indeed shifted to next year, though Netflix has neither confirmed this publicly nor is thought to have locked in a specific 2027 release window just yet." The article speculates that this is to brush up the VFX before release and move the show's finale away from other big releases, but there's no explicit confirmation as to why this delay has happened. It's a bummer if you've been chomping at the bit to see Liam Hemsworth totally witch all over the place, but since no major reshoots or further recasts have been confirmed, it's at least less grief than the God of War series is experiencing right now . title: Hit markers are an FPS crutch
summary: The humble hit marker has its place, but it's way overused.
body: Activision Id Software Crytek You've been shot, and I have the hit marker to prove it. FOV 90 (Image credit: Future) Welcome to FOV 90, an FPS column from staff writer Morgan Park. Every other week, I cover topics relevant to first-person shooter enjoyers, spanning everything from multiplayer and singleplayer to the old and the new. The humble hit marker glyph is a mainstay of the FPS user interface, dutifully reporting the fate of projectiles. Hit your target and 'X' marks the spot. See nothing, and you're hitting nothing. I like the hit marker—it's an absolute form of feedback unique to shooters, and I can think of a lot of games that wouldn't feel right without it. But it's also a crutch. The hit marker is both overused and often misused, nowadays appearing in every game with a gun as if it's always the best form of communication. The mechanic has even penetrated the singleplayer arena, which is weird, because the studio that popularized the hit marker always meant it to be a multiplayer-only concession. There are earlier examples of a hit marker, but it was made famous by Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare. The 'X' glyph and gratifying "thwip" sound instantly became iconic to the …

title: Bethesda 40th anniversary sale knocks 50% off Doom: The Dark Ages - Revelations just a month after launch

body: Bethesda is currently running a 40th anniversary sale on Steam until August 13, just in time for this year's QuakeCon. Former PCG guides writer Rory Norris awarded it a 90% in his review , while staff writer Morgan Park, who was more cold on Dark Ages' base game, argued that Revelations redeems the whole endeavor . title: The indie parkour game from one of the French brothers behind 2024's best FPS is coming out in just two weeks
summary: Mirror's Edge, Hot Lava, and surf map enjoyers may want to keep an eye on Vholume.
body: When I open up a trailer for a parkour game, I expect breakbeats or bassy electronica. You know, something radical —Vholume zigs where other games zag, scoring its run 'em up action with dejected, atmospheric synths punctuated by lonely footsteps and effortful grunts. A self-billed "melancholic first-person parkour adventure," it looks like the moody stepchild of Mirror's Edge. A new trailer for the game dropped last month and revealed it comes out Aug. 21. It provides a sneak peek at the game's overgrown, brutalist jungle gyms and shows off Vholume's multiplayer. According to its Steam page , you can race your buds in real time or compete against their ghosts. It seems ambitious given that just three people are credited as developers on Steam, one of whom you may recognize as one of the Lemaitre Bros. behind Straftat . We called that game 2024's best FPS, and its music is, in fact, radical . I hear the kids are really into liminality these days, so Vholume's dystopian dream world should appeal to anyone who saw Backrooms and felt like, for the first time in a long time, they were right where they were supposed to be. It also honors the parkour game tradition of being overtly anti…

title: WoW developers reflect on Midnight's first season—a world without AddOns, task overload, and Prey
summary: Curse of Ul'atek comes out next week, but how has Midnight's first season gone in the eyes of its devs?
body: Terminally Online (Image credit: Future) This is Terminally Online : PC Gamer's very own MMO column. Every other week, I'll be sharing my thoughts on the genre, interviewing fellow MMO-heads like me, taking a deep-dive into mechanics we've all taken for granted, and, occasionally, bringing in guest writers to talk about their MMO of choice. World of Warcraft: Midnight 's first season has been… well, a bit of a mixed bag. While the launch-day offerings impressed me, patch content—the major thing that gets remembered in the expansion pack history books—has ranged from rather quite good to downright confusing ( I still do not like the Folio ). And, to be fair, Midnight had a ton riding on it. It's the middle child of WoW's ambitious Worldsoul Saga and the first expansion where combat AddOns have been heavily hamstrung . As a consequence, every spec in the game was redesigned in some way . After 20 years of waiting, we even got p layer housing . title: Forget Quake, Worms: The Director's Cut just got a free expansion for the series' 30th anniversary
summary: Creator Andy Davidson hopes it gives the game "a new lease on life."
body: If you've checked in on Worms creator Andy Davidson sometime in these past few years, you'll know he's been hard at work on Worms: The Director's Cut 1.5 , an unofficial but nonetheless Team 17-approved expansion pack for the original strategy-party mashup's Amiga-exclusive sequel. The goods have finally arrived: you can download the whole thing for free now. It's got over 40 custom levels, 50 new sample packs for your Worms' voices, new teams and terrain types, and so on. It's a collaboration with fan creators and the likes of legendary indie developer Jeff Minter, who was honored via a Llamasoft-themed level in-game. In an interview with Daryl Baxter , Davidson called the expansion a chance to "celebrate the Amiga." "The expansion pack is a chance for people to enjoy the full package of DC, with all it could do. Rather than closing a chapter, I hope it gives the game a new lease on life," he told Baxter, saying work is underway on a site players can use to share custom levels. "It would be nice for a wider audience to get a chance to play DC. It’s the version of Worms I’m most proud of, as I feel it’s when the gameplay and humour really clicked."
